title: What is the "pinball architecture" / chained-choreography anti-pattern (a complex multi-step workflow modeled purely as reactive events chained across many services with no coordinator), why is it dangerous (you can't observe the workflow state or handle compensations), and when should you switch to an orchestrated Saga with a central state machine (e.g. Spring State Machine / Temporal / Camunda) that owns the steps and compensating transactions?

s1_definition.profdef: The pinball architecture, or chained-choreography anti-pattern, is what happens when a complex, multi-step business workflow is modeled purely as reactive events bouncing from one service to the next with no coordinator, so a request ricochets through many services like a ball in a pinball machine and no component owns or can see the overall flow. It is dangerous because you cannot observe the workflow's current state, you cannot easily tell which step failed, and you cannot cleanly handle compensations, since rollback logic is smeared across every service's failure handlers. The remedy is to switch to an orchestrated Saga with a central state machine — implemented with a tool like Spring State Machine, Temporal, or Camunda — that explicitly owns the steps and the compensating transactions.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a loan application at National Bank of India where each department just reacts to the previous one and flings the file onward with no manager overseeing it. Intake flings it to verification, verification flings it to credit scoring, credit scoring flings it to approval, approval flings it to disbursement — like a pinball bouncing off bumpers. When a customer asks "where is my loan application," nobody can answer, because no one is tracking it. And when disbursement fails, there is no manager to say "undo the approval, unfreeze the reserved funds"; each department has to guess how to clean up. Replacing the pinball machine with a case manager who holds the file, knows every step, and handles any rollback is the orchestrated Saga.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pinball architecture is a complex workflow bouncing through services with no coordinator, which destroys observability and compensation — the fix is an orchestrated Saga with a central state machine that owns the steps and rollbacks.

The remedy is to switch to an orchestrated Saga with a central state machine — implemented with a tool like Spring State Machine, Temporal, or Camunda — that explicitly owns the steps and the compensating transactions.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a loan application at National Bank of India where each department just reacts to the previous one and flings the file onward with no manager overseeing it. Intake flings it to verification, verification flings it to credit scoring, credit scoring flings it to approval, approval flings it to disbursement — like a pinball bouncing off bumpers. When a customer asks "where is my loan application," nobody can answer, because no one is tracking it. Replacing the pinball machine with a case manager who holds the file, knows every step, and handles any rollback is the orchestrated Saga.

**One line to remember:** Pinball architecture is a complex workflow bouncing through services with no coordinator, which destroys observability and compensation — the fix is an orchestrated Saga with a central state machine that owns the steps and rollbacks.

sections.s2_technical:
Choreography is a legitimate and valuable pattern for simple, independent reactions, but the pinball anti-pattern is what you get when you push choreography far past its comfort zone and model a genuinely complex, ordered, stateful workflow as a long chain of events across many services. Service A finishes and emits an event, B reacts and emits another, C reacts and emits another, and so on through many hops, with each service only knowing its own slice. The flow is implicit, scattered across subscriptions, and owned by no one. For a two- or three-step independent fan-out this is fine; for a seven-step ordered process with money and rollbacks, it becomes a nightmare.

The first danger is loss of observability. Because no component holds the workflow state, there is no single place to ask "what state is this order in" or "how far did this loan application get." Reconstructing the state means stitching together logs and events from many services after the fact, which is slow and error-prone, and it makes answering a customer's simple status question genuinely hard. You also cannot easily see where a flow stalled or how many are stuck at a given step.

The second danger is broken failure handling and compensation. In a complex flow, when a late step fails you must undo the earlier committed steps in the right order. With pinball choreography there is no coordinator to drive that rollback, so each service has to subscribe to failure events and implement its own compensation reactively, which spreads the error-handling logic across the whole system, makes the compensation order implicit and fragile, and makes it very hard to guarantee that every partially completed flow is cleaned up correctly. Missed or out-of-order compensations leave money or inventory in a bad state.

The third danger is unmanageable coupling and change. The chain of "who reacts to whose event" becomes a hidden dependency graph that nobody fully understands, so changing the flow — inserting a step, reordering, adding a branch — risks breaking it in non-obvious ways, and testing the end-to-end behavior is difficult because there is no single entry point that represents the workflow.

The remedy is to switch to an orchestrated Saga with a central state machine. You introduce an orchestrator that owns the workflow definition explicitly: it knows the ordered steps, invokes each service in turn, records the state after each step in durable storage, and on failure drives the compensating transactions in the correct reverse order. A dedicated workflow engine makes this robust — Spring State Machine for lighter in-service state machines, or Temporal and Camunda for durable, long-running workflows with built-in retries, timeouts, versioning, and visibility. Now the workflow state is a first-class, queryable thing, failures are handled in one understandable place, and the flow can be changed, tested, and observed as a unit.

A senior engineer frames the decision as matching coordination to workflow complexity. Keep choreography for simple, short, independent reactions where its decoupling shines. Switch to orchestration the moment the workflow becomes complex, ordered, and stateful, or needs real compensations and observable status — which is exactly when pinball choreography would otherwise emerge. The warning sign to watch for is a business process whose state you cannot answer from any single place and whose rollback logic is scattered across failure listeners; that is the signal to put a state machine in charge.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India models a loan disbursement as a five-step workflow — application, verification, credit scoring, approval, disbursement — and initially builds it as pure chained choreography.

Problem 1 — Each service only reacts to the previous event and emits the next, so when a customer asks "where is my loan," no component can answer, because nobody tracks the state. This is the observability failure of pinball architecture.

Problem 2 — When disbursement fails, the earlier steps (approval recorded, funds reserved) must be undone, but there is no coordinator, so each service would have to react to a failure event and guess its compensation. The rollback is scattered and fragile. This is the compensation failure.

Problem 3 — The fix is an orchestrated Saga. A `LoanOrchestrator` with an explicit state machine calls each step in order, records the state, and on disbursement failure drives the compensations in reverse — unreserve funds, revoke approval — from one place, and can answer the loan's current state at any time.

What the code will do: a runnable demo first implements `PinballChoreography`, where services bounce events with no coordinator and a status query cannot determine the state, and failure handling is shown to be scattered. Then it implements `LoanOrchestrator`, a central state machine that tracks state, exposes a `getState()` query, runs the steps, and on failure runs ordered compensations, demonstrating the switch.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a loan LOAN-1 run under pinball choreography, and LOAN-2 run under the orchestrated Saga with disbursement forced to fail.

Step 1 (pinball): Verification runs and publishes Verified. Credit scoring reacts and publishes Scored. Approval reacts and publishes Approved. Disbursement reacts, reserves funds, and publishes FundsReserved. The loan has bounced through four services, each knowing only its slice.

Step 2 (pinball): A status query asks where LOAN-1 is. No component holds the state, so the answer is UNKNOWN. This is the observability failure.

Step 3 (pinball): Disbursement fails. There is no coordinator, so the single disbursement service tries to handle the rollback itself, but the compensation order and ownership are unclear and scattered — approval and reserved funds may not be cleanly undone. This is the compensation failure.

Step 4 (orchestration): The orchestrator processes LOAN-2, calling verify, score, approve, and reserve funds in order, recording the state after each step in its durable map, so the state is always known.

Step 5 (orchestration): Disbursement fails. The orchestrator catches it, sets state to COMPENSATING, and drives the compensations in the correct reverse order from one place — release funds, then revoke approval — and ends in CANCELLED.

Step 6 (orchestration): A status query for LOAN-2 returns CANCELLED immediately, because the orchestrator holds the state. Observability and clean compensation are both restored.

Final output:

```
17:30:00 INFO    ===== PINBALL CHOREOGRAPHY (anti-pattern) =====

17:30:00 INFO    [APPROVE] LOAN-1
17:30:00 INFO    [FUNDS] reserved for LOAN-1
17:30:00 SEVERE  [DISBURSE] FAILED for LOAN-1
17:30:00 SEVERE  [PINBALL] disbursement failed — compensation logic scattered, order unclear
17:30:00 SEVERE  [STATUS] where is LOAN-1? → UNKNOWN (no component holds the state)
17:30:00 INFO    ===== ORCHESTRATED SAGA (fix: central state machine) =====
17:30:00 INFO    [VERIFY] LOAN-2
17:30:00 INFO    [SCORE] LOAN-2
17:30:00 INFO    [APPROVE] LOAN-2
17:30:00 INFO    [FUNDS] reserved for LOAN-2
17:30:00 SEVERE  [DISBURSE] FAILED for LOAN-2
17:30:00 SEVERE  [ORCH] disbursement failed → central ordered compensation

17:30:00 WARNING [APPROVE] compensate revoke LOAN-2

```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── PINBALL (anti-pattern) ──
  Verify ─Verified→ Score ─Scored→ Approve ─Approved→ Disburse(reserve) ─FundsReserved→ Disburse(pay)
                                                                                          │ FAIL
  no coordinator → state UNKNOWN; compensation scattered in each service's listener  ✗
  "where is LOAN-1?" → nobody can answer

  ── ORCHESTRATED SAGA (fix) ──
  LoanOrchestrator (state machine, durable state)
    │ verify     → state=VERIFIED
    │ score      → state=SCORED
    │ approve    → state=APPROVED
    │ reserve + disburse
    │     └─ FAIL → state=COMPENSATING
    │              release funds → revoke approval (ordered, one place)
    │              → state=CANCELLED
    ▼
  getState(LOAN-2) → CANCELLED  (observable anytime)  ✓
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The pinball architecture, or chained-choreography anti-pattern, is what happens when a genuinely complex, multi-step, stateful workflow is modeled purely as reactive events bouncing from service to service with no coordinator. A request ricochets through many services like a ball off pinball bumpers — A emits an event, B reacts and emits another, C reacts and emits another — and each service knows only its own slice, so the overall flow is implicit, scattered across subscriptions, and owned by no one. Choreography is perfectly good for simple, short, independent reactions, but pushing it onto a seven-step process with money and rollbacks is where it turns into pinball.

It is dangerous for three concrete reasons. First, observability collapses: because no component holds the workflow state, there is no single place to answer what state an order or a loan is in or where it failed, and reconstructing that from logs and events across many services is slow and error-prone. Second, failure handling and compensation break down: in a complex flow a late failure must undo earlier committed steps in the right order, but with no coordinator each service has to react to failure events and implement its own compensation, which smears the rollback logic across the whole system, makes the compensation order implicit and fragile, and makes it very hard to guarantee every partial flow is cleaned up. Third, the chain of who-reacts-to-whom becomes a hidden dependency web nobody fully understands, so changing or testing the flow is risky.

The remedy is to switch to an orchestrated Saga with a central state machine. I introduce an orchestrator that owns the workflow definition explicitly — it knows the ordered steps, invokes each service in turn, records the state after each step in durable storage, and on failure drives the compensating transactions in the correct reverse order from one place. For robustness I use a workflow engine: Spring State Machine for lighter in-service machines, or Temporal and Camunda for durable long-running workflows with built-in retries, timeouts, versioning, and visibility. Now the workflow state is a first-class, queryable thing, failures are handled in one understandable place, and the flow can be changed, tested, and observed as a unit.

I lived this at National Bank of India with loan disbursement, a five-step flow of verification, scoring, approval, fund reservation, and disbursement. We first built it as chained choreography, and it bit us hard: when a customer asked where their loan was, nobody could answer because no component tracked the state, and when disbursement failed, the rollback of the approval and the reserved funds was scattered and sometimes incomplete. We switched to an orchestrated Saga with a central state machine that recorded the state after every step and, on a disbursement failure, released the reserved funds and revoked the approval in order from one place, and we could answer the loan's current state instantly. The flow became observable and its compensation reliable.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is this: pinball architecture is a complex workflow bouncing through services as chained events with no coordinator, which destroys your ability to observe the state or compensate cleanly on failure, so when a process is complex, ordered, stateful, or needs real rollbacks, I switch from choreography to an orchestrated Saga with a central state machine — Temporal, Camunda, or Spring State Machine — that owns the steps and the compensating transactions.
